items.q: A functional dependency X → Y means:
options: X and Y have the same values
items.explain: **X → Y**: any two tuples agreeing on **X** must agree on **Y**. X is the *determinant*. Note the direction is not symmetric — X → Y says nothing about whether Y → X.

items.q: If X is a candidate key of relation R, which is true?
options: X → Y holds for no subset Y
X → R does not necessarily hold
items.explain: A candidate key **functionally determines every attribute of the relation** — that is what being a key *means*, so **X → R**. The 'candidate' part adds minimality: no proper subset of X also determines R.

items.q: Which of the following is a **partial** dependency?
options: {Ssn, Pnumber} → Ename, where Ssn → Ename also holds
items.explain: A **partial dependency** is a non-prime attribute determined by **part of a composite key**. With key `{Ssn, Pnumber}`, `Ename` really depends on **Ssn alone** — so it is partial, and it violates **2NF**. `Hours` needs *both* key parts, so that one is a full dependency.

items.q: Which dependency is **trivial**?
items.explain: An FD X → Y is **trivial** when **Y ⊆ X**. In `ABC → BC`, the right side is contained in the left, so it holds in *every* relation and carries no information. (`A → AB` is not trivial — `B` is not in `{A}`.)

items.q: For a relation with attributes (A, B, C, D), which set of FDs indicates a **transitive** dependency?
items.explain: A **transitive dependency** is a chain **key → non-prime → non-prime**. With `A` as the key, `A → B → C` makes `C` depend on the key only *through* `B`. That is what **3NF** forbids. (Option 4 has the same shape but `B → A` where A is the key, which is a different situation.)

items.q: According to Armstrong's axioms, which rule states that if Y ⊆ X then X → Y?
items.explain: **Reflexivity** generates exactly the **trivial** dependencies. The three axioms are: **Reflexivity** (Y ⊆ X ⇒ X → Y), **Augmentation** (X → Y ⇒ XZ → YZ), **Transitivity** (X → Y and Y → Z ⇒ X → Z). Union, decomposition and pseudo-transitivity are derived from these.

items.q: Which inference rule lets you infer WX → Z from X → Y and WY → Z?
items.explain: **Pseudo-transitivity**: X → Y and WY → Z ⇒ WX → Z. Intuitively, X supplies Y, and W together with Y supplies Z — so W together with X suffices. It is derivable: augment X → Y with W to get WX → WY, then apply transitivity with WY → Z.

items.q: Given F = {A → BC, CD → EF}, which FD can be inferred?
items.explain: Compute **{AD}⁺**: start {A, D} → `A → BC` adds B, C → now {A, B, C, D} contains both C and D, so `CD → EF` adds E, F → **{A, B, C, D, E, F}**. F is present, so **AD → F** holds. `A⁺` is only {A, B, C} — without D the second FD never fires, so `A → EF` fails.

items.q: R(A, B, C, D, E, F) with F = {A → BC, B → E, CD → EF}. Which FD can be inferred?
items.explain: **{AD}⁺** = {A, D} → +BC → {A, B, C, D} → `B → E` adds E → `CD → EF` adds F → **all six attributes**, so `AD → F` holds. Check the others: `A⁺` = {A, B, C, E} (no F), `{CD}⁺` = {C, D, E, F} (no A), and `B⁺` = {B, E} (no C).

items.q: Which property ensures that no information is lost when a relation is decomposed into two relations?
items.explain: **Lossless join** (non-additive join): re-joining the fragments returns **exactly** the original relation — no spurious extra tuples. For a binary decomposition into R₁ and R₂ the test is simple: **R₁ ∩ R₂ must be a superkey of R₁ or of R₂**. Dependency preservation is the *other*, independent goal.

items.q: The closure of a set of functional dependencies F, written F⁺, is:
options: The set of all trivial dependencies
The set of all dependencies in F only
The set of all dependencies logically implied by F
The set of all candidate keys
items.explain: **F⁺ is everything F entails**, obtained by applying Armstrong's axioms until nothing new appears. Distinguish it from **X⁺** (*attribute* closure) — the set of attributes determined by X. F⁺ is usually huge; X⁺ is what you actually compute by hand.

items.q: If A → B and B → H, which dependency holds?
items.explain: **Transitivity** gives **A → H**. The reverse directions (`H → A`, `B → A`) do *not* follow — functional dependency is **not symmetric**, and assuming it is causes more normalization errors than any other single mistake.

items.q: R(A, B, C, G, H, I) with F = {A → B, A → C, CG → H, CG → I, B → H}. Which is implied by F?
items.explain: **A⁺** = {A} → `A → B`, `A → C` add B, C → `B → H` adds H → **{A, B, C, H}**. So **A → H** holds. The others fail: `C⁺` = {C} and `G⁺` = {G}, because **`CG → I` needs C *and* G together** — a composite left side never fires on half its attributes.

items.q: In the algorithm for computing X⁺ under F, what condition adds new attributes to X⁺?
options: If Z ⊆ X for some FD Y → Z
If there is an FD Y → Z with Y ⊆ X⁺, then add Z to X⁺
If there is an FD Y → Z with Z ⊆ X⁺, then add Y to X⁺
If X⁺ ⊆ Y for some FD Y → Z
items.explain: Repeat until nothing changes: **if the whole left side of an FD is already inside X⁺, add its right side**. Two traps — the left side must be **fully** contained (a composite LHS needs *all* its attributes), and you must **re-scan every FD after each addition**, since a newly added attribute can unlock earlier ones.

items.q: Given F = {AB → CD, AF → D, DE → F, C → G, F → E, G → A}, what is **{AF}⁺**?
items.explain: Start **{A, F}** → `AF → D` adds **D** → `F → E` adds **E** → now {A, D, E, F}. Check the rest: `DE → F` (F already there), `AB → CD` needs **B** — absent, `C → G` needs **C** — absent, `G → A` needs **G** — absent. Nothing more fires, so **{AF}⁺ = {A, D, E, F}**. Since it misses B, C and G, AF is **not** a key.

items.q: Given F = {AB → CD, AF → D, DE → F, C → G, F → E, G → A}, what is **{BG}⁺**?
options: {A, B, C, D, E, F, G}
items.explain: Start **{B, G}** → `G → A` adds **A** → now A and B are both present so `AB → CD` adds **C, D** → `C → G` (already there). `DE → F` needs **E** — absent; `F → E` needs F — absent. Result: **{A, B, C, D, G}**.

items.q: What does it mean when we say that F **covers** G?
options: Every FD in G can be inferred from F
F and G have the same number of FDs
Every FD in F can be inferred from G
items.explain: **F covers G** ⟺ **G ⊆ F⁺** — F is strong enough to derive everything G says. Note the direction carefully; it is the reverse of what the wording suggests to many students. The number of FDs is irrelevant: a two-FD set can cover a ten-FD set.

items.q: To determine whether F covers G, you must:
options: Compute the closure of all attributes in F
For each FD X → Y in G, compute X⁺ under F and check that Y ⊆ X⁺
Compare the number of dependencies in F and G
Decompose all FDs into canonical form first
items.explain: For **every** FD in G, compute the left side's closure **using F**, and confirm the right side is inside it. If even one fails, F does not cover G. You never need to build F⁺ itself — attribute closure is the practical tool.

items.q: Two sets of functional dependencies F and G are **equivalent** if:
options: F covers G AND G covers F (equivalently, F⁺ = G⁺)
They contain the same number of FDs
items.explain: Equivalence requires **coverage in both directions**, which is the same as saying **F⁺ = G⁺** — the two sets constrain the data identically even if they look nothing alike. One-directional coverage is strictly weaker.

items.q: FD1 = {A → B, B → C, AB → D} and FD2 = {A → B, B → C, A → C, A → D}. What is their relationship?
items.explain: **FD1 covers FD2:** under FD1, `A⁺` = {A, B, C, D} (A→B, B→C, then AB→D fires since A and B are both present) — so `A → C` and `A → D` both hold. **FD2 covers FD1:** under FD2, `{AB}⁺` = {A, B, C, D}, so `AB → D` holds. Both directions succeed, so they are **equivalent**.

items.q: F = {A → C, AC → D, E → AD, E → H} and G = {A → CD, E → AH}. Which is true?
items.explain: **F ⊨ G:** `A⁺` under F = {A, C, D} ⊇ {C, D} ✓; `E⁺` under F = {E, A, D, H, C} ⊇ {A, H} ✓. **G ⊨ F:** `A⁺` under G = {A, C, D} covers `A → C` and `AC → D` ✓; `E⁺` under G = {E, A, H, C, D} covers `E → AD` and `E → H` ✓. Both ways hold, so **F = G**.

items.q: What is a **minimal cover** of a set of functional dependencies?
options: A set where all attributes are superkeys
A set that contains redundant attributes
A set of dependencies with multiple attributes on the RHS
A minimal set of dependencies equivalent to the original set
items.explain: A **minimal (canonical) cover** is the smallest FD set with the **same closure** as the original — no redundant FDs, no extraneous left-side attributes, single attribute on each right side. It is the standard preprocessing step before **3NF synthesis**.

items.q: Which is NOT a property of a minimal cover?
options: Every dependency has a single attribute on the RHS
No functional dependency can be removed without changing the closure
No attribute can be removed from a LHS without changing the closure
All dependencies must have more than one attribute on the LHS
items.explain: There is **no requirement about the size of the left side** — minimality *shrinks* left sides where possible, so single-attribute LHSs are common and perfectly valid. The other three are exactly the three conditions: singleton RHS, no redundant FD, no extraneous LHS attribute.

items.q: For E = {B → A, D → A, AB → D}, which dependency turns out to be redundant in the minimal cover?
items.explain: First reduce the left side of `AB → D`: since **B → A**, `B⁺` = {A, B} already contains A, so **A is extraneous** and the FD becomes **B → D**. Now re-test `B → A` for redundancy: without it, `B⁺` = {B} → `B → D` adds D → `D → A` adds **A**. It is derivable, so **B → A is redundant**. Minimal cover: **{B → D, D → A}**.

items.q: In F = {A → C, AB → C, C → D, CD → I, EC → AB, EI → C}, which FD is redundant?
items.explain: **`AB → C` is implied by `A → C`** — augment `A → C` with B to get `AB → BC`, then decompose. Equivalently, `{AB}⁺` computed **without** `AB → C` still contains C. The others are each the sole source of their right-hand attributes: drop `EI → C` and `{EI}⁺` = {E, I}, with no way to reach C.

items.q: For R(A, B, C, D, E, F) with F = {C → F, E → A, EC → D, A → B}, what is the only candidate key?
items.explain: **Attributes appearing on no right-hand side must be in every key.** RHS attributes here are {F, A, D, B}, so **C and E** appear nowhere on the right and must be in the key. Test `{EC}⁺`: {C, E} → +F (C→F) → +A (E→A) → +D (EC→D) → +B (A→B) = **all six attributes**. Since {C, E} alone suffices, **EC is the unique candidate key**.

items.q: What is the main goal of normalization?
options: To store data in nested form
To increase redundancy for faster access
To reduce redundancy and eliminate insertion, update and deletion anomalies
items.explain: Normalization removes **redundancy** and with it the three **anomalies**: *insertion* (cannot record a department without an employee), *update* (change a fact in one row but not its copies), *deletion* (removing the last employee erases the department). It is a **correctness** technique, not a performance one.

items.q: Which is true for a relation in **First Normal Form (1NF)**?
options: Every attribute contains only atomic (indivisible) values
items.explain: **1NF demands atomic values** — no repeating groups, no sets inside a cell, no nested relations. This is why a multivalued ER attribute such as `Color` must become its **own relation** during reduction; leaving it as a comma-separated list breaks 1NF.

items.q: Which correctly describes **Second Normal Form (2NF)**?
options: Every attribute is a foreign key
Every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on every candidate key
No attribute depends transitively on the key
items.explain: **2NF = 1NF + no partial dependencies** — no non-prime attribute may depend on only *part* of a composite key. Corollary worth remembering: **if every candidate key is a single attribute, the relation is automatically in 2NF**, because there is no 'part of a key' to depend on.

items.q: R(SSN, PNUMBER, HOURS, ENAME) with {SSN, PNUMBER} → HOURS and SSN → ENAME. Which is correct?
options: R is not in 2NF because of a partial dependency
items.explain: The key is **{SSN, PNUMBER}**, so `ENAME` is non-prime — yet it depends on **SSN alone**, half the key. That is a **partial dependency**, so R is **1NF but not 2NF**. The fix is to split: `WORKS_ON(SSN, PNUMBER, HOURS)` and `EMPLOYEE(SSN, ENAME)`.

items.q: R(A, B, C) with FDs {A → B, B → C}. Which is true?
options: R is in 2NF but not in 3NF
items.explain: The only candidate key is **A** (`A⁺` = {A, B, C}). Because the key is a **single attribute**, no partial dependency is possible → **2NF holds**. But `B → C` with B non-prime is a **transitive dependency** (A → B → C) → **3NF fails**. Highest normal form: **2NF**.

items.q: Which is a violation of 3NF?
options: A non-prime attribute depending on a candidate key
A non-prime attribute depending on another non-prime attribute (transitive dependency)
A prime attribute depending on a superkey
items.explain: **3NF forbids transitive dependencies**: for every non-trivial X → A, either **X is a superkey** or **A is prime**. A non-prime attribute determined by another non-prime attribute satisfies neither escape clause. Option 1 is exactly what a well-normalized relation *should* look like.

items.q: In BCNF, if a non-trivial functional dependency X → A holds in R, then:
options: X must be a candidate key
A must be a prime attribute
items.explain: **BCNF: every determinant must be a superkey.** 'Superkey' rather than 'candidate key' is the precise wording — a candidate key with extra attributes attached is still a superkey and still fine. **BCNF is 3NF minus the 'or A is prime' escape clause**, which is exactly why it is stricter.

items.q: TEACH(student, course, instructor) with {student, course} → instructor and instructor → course. Which normal form does it satisfy?
items.explain: Candidate keys are **{student, course}** and **{student, instructor}** — so **all three attributes are prime**, and with no non-prime attributes at all, 2NF and 3NF hold automatically. But **`instructor → course` has a determinant that is not a superkey**, so **BCNF fails**. This is the textbook case where 3NF and BCNF diverge — and where a BCNF decomposition would **lose** the dependency `{student, course} → instructor`.

items.q: A relation schema R is in **4NF** if:
options: Every non-prime attribute depends only on the primary key
For every non-trivial multivalued dependency X ↠ Y, X is a superkey
Every functional dependency has X as a superkey
items.explain: **4NF** extends BCNF's rule from functional to **multivalued** dependencies: every non-trivial **X ↠ Y** must have **X as a superkey**. Option 3 is BCNF's condition — 4NF is the same shape of rule applied to MVDs.

items.q: A multivalued dependency X ↠ Y in R is **trivial** if:
options: Either Y ⊆ X or X ∪ Y = R
items.explain: **Both** conditions make an MVD trivial — either the right side is contained in the left, **or** together they exhaust the relation's attributes. A trivial MVD holds in every instance, so 4NF only constrains the **non-trivial** ones.

items.q: EMP(Ename, Pname, Dname) with MVDs Ename ↠ Pname and Ename ↠ Dname. Which is correct?
options: EMP is in 3NF but not BCNF
EMP is in BCNF but not 4NF
items.explain: The only key is **all three attributes**, and there are no non-trivial *functional* dependencies — so **BCNF holds vacuously**. But `Ename ↠ Pname` is a **non-trivial MVD whose determinant is not a superkey**, so **4NF fails**. The symptom is the classic one: independent projects and dependents get multiplied together, forcing a row for every combination.

items.q: Which statement about the normal-form hierarchy is TRUE?
options: Every relation in BCNF is in 4NF
Every relation in 4NF is in BCNF
items.explain: The hierarchy is **strictly nested downward**: 1NF ⊃ 2NF ⊃ 3NF ⊃ BCNF ⊃ 4NF ⊃ 5NF. So a **higher** form implies all lower ones — 4NF ⇒ BCNF. The reverse never holds: the EMP example above is in BCNF but **not** 4NF.

items.q: Which statement about **5NF** is correct?
options: An MVD is a special case of a join dependency into three parts
Discovering join dependencies in large databases is straightforward
5NF is the normal form most commonly enforced in practice
A relation is in 5NF if every non-trivial join dependency has each Ri as a superkey
items.explain: **5NF (project-join normal form)** requires every non-trivial **join dependency** to be implied by the candidate keys — each component Rᵢ being a superkey. An **MVD is the special case of a JD with *two* components**, not three. And JDs are notoriously **hard to discover**, which is why 5NF is rarely enforced in practice — most designs stop at 3NF or BCNF.

items.q: The main goal of query optimization is to:
options: Find the most efficient query-evaluation plan
Reduce the size of the query text
items.explain: SQL is **declarative** — you state *what* you want, not *how*. Many equivalent execution plans exist, and the optimizer's job is to pick the **cheapest** using catalog statistics. Redundancy and schema simplification are **normalization** concerns, a different topic entirely.

items.q: The EXPLAIN statement in MySQL is used to:
options: Show how MySQL plans to execute a query
Create a view of the query
items.explain: **EXPLAIN reveals the execution plan** — join order, access method per table, which index (if any) is chosen, and estimated row counts. It does **not run** the query. (`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` does run it and reports actual timings.)

items.q: Which value in EXPLAIN output indicates a potential performance problem?
items.explain: **`type = ALL` means a full table scan** — every row is read because no usable index exists. The access types run roughly best-to-worst: `const` → `eq_ref` → `ref` → `range` → `index` → **`ALL`**. Seeing `ALL` on a large table is the classic signal that an index is missing.

items.q: Which optimization technique divides a table by rows or columns to improve performance?
items.explain: **Partitioning** splits one logical table into physical pieces — **horizontal** (by rows, e.g. one partition per year) or **vertical** (by columns). The payoff is **partition pruning**: a query filtered to 2024 touches only that partition and skips the rest.

items.q: Replacing correlated subqueries with joins is beneficial because:
options: A join is evaluated as a single set-based operation, while a correlated subquery re-executes per outer row
items.explain: A correlated subquery is conceptually a **nested loop** — re-evaluated for **every** outer row. Rewritten as a join, the optimizer can choose a **hash or merge join** and process the whole set at once. Note 'always' claims are wrong: a hash join may well use *more* memory, it is simply faster.

items.q: What are the three main steps of query processing?
items.explain: **Parsing and translation** turns SQL into a relational-algebra expression (checking syntax and catalog references), **optimization** picks the cheapest equivalent evaluation plan, and **evaluation** runs it against the stored data. Query optimization matters because the cost gap between the best and worst plans for one query can be orders of magnitude.

items.q: A relation stores `Dname` alongside every employee row, repeated for all employees of a department. Which anomaly appears when the last employee of a department is deleted?
options: No anomaly — the design is fine
items.explain: **Deletion anomaly** — removing that final employee row erases the **only record that the department exists**. The same design also produces an *insertion* anomaly (you cannot register a new department before hiring someone) and an *update* anomaly (renaming a department means editing every one of its employee rows). All three come from one cause: **two independent facts crammed into one relation**.
